1.story: The hoopoe and the queen of Sheba's letter, Qur'an 27:20-31 (the bismillah at 27:30)
1.point: Bismillah means 'in the name of God': Muslims start things with it, so nothing begins alone.
1.script: A small bird, a hoopoe, went missing, then came back with news. Far south, in Sheba, a queen sat on a mighty throne, and her people bowed to the sun. So the prophet Solomon sent the bird back, with a letter. It dropped the letter before the queen. She broke the seal and read it to her court. The most powerful king alive, and his letter didn't open with his own name. It opened: in the name of God, the Beneficent, the Merciful. That's bismillah. All but one surah of the Qur'an opens with it. Muslims say it before a meal, a drive, an exam. So you never start alone.

open.text: a king's letter opened with *another* name.

2.story: The scorpion-stung chief healed with al-Fatiha, Sahih al-Bukhari 5749 / Sahih Muslim 2201; with the hadith qudsi of the prayer as a conversation, Sahih Muslim 395
2.point: Al-Fatiha, the opening, is seven verses said in every prayer: mostly praise, one request (show us the straight path), and described as a conversation with God.
2.script: A band of travelers, companions of the Prophet, reached a desert camp and asked for food. The tribe said no. Then their chief was stung by a scorpion. Nothing they tried worked. So they came running back: can any of you do something? One traveler knelt by the chief and recited seven short verses. The chief stood up and walked. Those seven verses? Every Muslim says them in every prayer. Al-Fatiha, the opening. Mostly praise, then one request: show us the straight path. A saying of the Prophet calls it a conversation, with God answering, line by line. Those words you've heard a thousand times? Someone answers them.

open.text: seven short verses. the chief *stood up.*

3.story: Bilal's footsteps heard in Paradise, Sahih al-Bukhari 1149 / Sahih Muslim 2458; with the hadith of wrongs leaving with the water, Sahih Muslim 244
3.point: Wudu, the washing before prayer, is a reset that isn't about dirt: as the water runs off, the wrongs run off with it.
3.script: Bilal had once been enslaved, punished in the desert sun for his faith. Freed, he became the first voice to call Muslims to prayer. One morning, the Prophet asked him a question. Bilal, what do you do? In Paradise, I heard your footsteps ahead of me. Bilal's answer was small. Every time I wash for prayer, day or night, I pray after it. That's all. That washing is wudu: hands, mouth, face, arms, head, feet. It isn't about dirt. People do it already clean. A saying of the Prophet says that as the water runs off, the wrongs run off with it. Rough day? Rinse it off.

4.story: The parable of the two gardens, Qur'an 18:32-44 (ma sha' Allah at 18:39), with the command to say 'if God wills', Qur'an 18:23-24
4.point: Inshallah ('if God wills') is for plans about tomorrow; mashallah ('what God has willed') is for good that's already here; both come from the same surah.
4.script: Two men. One owned two gardens: grapevines, date palms, a river running between them. He walked through with his friend and bragged. I have more than you. I don't think this will ever end. His friend asked one question. When you walked in, why didn't you say: mashallah? What God has willed. Then it was all gone. The vines collapsed on their trellises. He stood there, wringing his hands. That's in the Qur'an, in the surah called the Cave. The same surah says: never say I'll do it tomorrow without, if God wills. Inshallah. So, inshallah for tomorrow. Mashallah for what's already here. Plan it fully. Then hold it open.

open.text: he said it would *never* end. it did.

5.story: Ibrahim asks to see how God gives life to the dead, Qur'an 2:260; with the companions' troubling thoughts, 'that is clear faith', Sahih Muslim 132
5.point: Iman, faith, can grow and has room for questions: in the Qur'an a prophet asked to see so his heart could rest, and he wasn't turned away.
5.script: A man asked God for proof. Not just anyone: Ibrahim, Abraham, one of the greatest prophets. My Lord, show me how you give life to the dead. The Qur'an records the reply: do you not believe? Yes, he said. But so my heart can be at ease. He wasn't scolded. He was shown. Four birds, scattered across four hills. He called them, and they came flying back to him. Centuries later, the Prophet's companions confessed thoughts so dark they could barely say them. He told them: that is clear faith. Iman, faith, can grow. Questions are part of it. Ask, so your heart can rest.

open.text: a prophet *asked* for proof. and got it.

6.story: The first revelation in the cave of Hira, Sahih al-Bukhari 3 and Qur'an 96:1-5; Ramadan as the month the Qur'an was revealed, Qur'an 2:185; the fast's purpose, Qur'an 2:183
6.point: Ramadan is the month the Qur'an first came, so Muslims fast from dawn to sunset: not to suffer, but to grow mindful.
6.script: Outside Mecca there's a mountain with a small cave near the top. A man used to climb it to be alone, and think. One night, in Ramadan, tradition says, the silence broke. A voice: Read. He came down trembling. His wife Khadijah wrapped him in a cloak. That man was the Prophet Muhammad, and those were the first words of the Qur'an. That's why Ramadan matters. It's the month the Qur'an came. So Muslims fast, dawn to sunset: no food, not even water. Not to suffer. The Qur'an says it's so you'll be mindful. Then sunset. A date, some water. Hunger teaches you to notice.

open.text: one night, a cave, and one word: *read.*

7.story: The two old festival days of Medina replaced by two better ones, Sunan Abi Dawud 1134 / Sunan an-Nasa'i 1556; zakat al-fitr, Sahih al-Bukhari 1503; Ibrahim's ram, Qur'an 37:102-107; sharing the meat, Qur'an 22:36
7.point: Islam has two Eids, al-Fitr after Ramadan and al-Adha at the pilgrimage, and both are built so nobody is left out of the feast.
7.script: When the Prophet came to Medina, the city had two old festival days of games and fun. You might think a new faith would cancel them. It didn't. He told them God had given them two better days. The first, Eid al-Fitr, the day the Ramadan fast breaks. Before the prayer, every household gives food, so even the poorest family can feast. The second, Eid al-Adha, at the time of the pilgrimage. It remembers Ibrahim, and the ram given in place of his son. The meat is shared with family, neighbors, and people in need. Two Eids. New clothes, an envelope from an uncle. And nobody left out.

open.text: a new faith arrived. would it *cancel* the party?

Day 2: Sahih al-Bukhari 5749, 2276; Sahih Muslim 2201 (al-Fatiha recited over the stung chief); Qur'an 1:1-7; Sahih Muslim 395 (hadith qudsi: the prayer as a conversation); Sahih al-Bukhari 756 (no prayer without al-Fatiha)

risks: Depiction: every picture brief forbids any prophet or angel in any form, but painters (human or AI) often insert a glowing central figure in mosque, cave, prayer-ground and 'Ibrahim' scenes (day 3 pic 3, day 5 pics 1-4, day 6 pics 2-5, day 7 pics 1 and 3). Each output image must be checked by eye for any implied prophet, including a lone robed figure, light shaped like a person or a figure on a hilltop. Some Muslims also object to depicting senior companions (Bilal, Khadijah) or the Paradise garden even partially; a scholar should confirm whether distant silhouettes and hands are acceptable, or whether those shots should be objects only.

Day 1: the Qur'an does not name the queen (Bilqis is later tradition), so the script leaves her unnamed. 'The most powerful king alive' is narrator framing, not a Qur'anic phrase. Solomon's threat to the hoopoe (27:21) and the letter's full message (27:31) are left out.

Day 2: the hadith has the companions take a flock of sheep as payment and later ask the Prophet about it; that part is left out. 'Someone answers them' compresses the hadith qudsi of Sahih Muslim 395 (God answers each line of al-Fatiha); check the wording is acceptable.

Day 3: 'punished in the desert sun' for Bilal comes from the sira (Ibn Ishaq), not the Qur'an or the Bukhari hadith. The Paradise garden picture is an artistic image; some may prefer it not be painted at all.

Day 4: tying the 'Cave' (the surah's name) to a cave picture is fine, but day 4 pic 6 must not show the Sleepers of the Cave; the brief hints a sleeping dog only as a boulder. Confirm that is acceptable or drop the hint.

Day 5: 'four birds, scattered across four hills' simplifies 2:260. Most classical commentators say the birds were cut up and their parts placed on the hills; a minority (e.g. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani) read it as training the birds. The script avoids taking a side, but a scholar should confirm the wording. 'Centuries later' is roughly right in spirit but imprecise (Ibrahim's era is undated).

Day 6: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 does not give the month; that the first revelation came in Ramadan rests on Qur'an 2:185 and 97:1 plus sira tradition, hence 'tradition says'. The 'voice' was the angel Jibril; the script does not name him and no angel is shown. 'Not even water' and 'dawn to sunset' agree with the lesson.

Day 7: 'You might think a new faith would cancel them' is narrator framing. The son in the ram story is unnamed in the Qur'an (most Muslims say Ismail); the script says 'his son', matching the lesson. Some schools treat the Eid sacrifice as obligatory and others as strongly recommended; the script stays neutral.
